episodes.title: Bessent’s Bond Battle, Go Broad Not Bearish, and Stripe’s Strategy 8/20/26
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled the Treasury may expand long-bond buybacks beyond the announced $4bn minimum per issue, an unusual intervention aimed at illiquidity in off-the-run long-dated Treasuries. Yields backed up anyway, with the 10-year around 4.70% and the 30-year having just hit a decades-high 5.33%, undoing much of the prior day's rally — a dynamic directly relevant to global rates and USD positioning that EM trades against.

**Key points**
- Treasury will increase buyback size, potentially above the $4bn/issue minimum; framed as addressing summertime illiquidity, not yield suppression.
- Fiscal consolidation announcement teased for late this week/early next week with OMB director Russ Vought.
- Oil: WTI near $90/bbl after Trump declared an economic campaign against Iran, threatening sanctions on any country/entity aiding Iran's oil trade, explicitly including China's Iran trade; China gets ~50% of its energy from the Gulf.
- 10-year yield was sub-4% before the Iran-related escalation; oil-driven yield rise is a key transmission channel now.
- US fiscal deficit narrowed from 8% of GDP (2023) to 5.9% currently per Mitch Daniels citing Michael Darda, though debt stock is near $40 trillion.
- Guest (First Eagle's Matt McClennan) flagged "fiscal risk in the world's reserve currency" (USD) as the defining 2020s theme, favoring gold and real/scarce assets over concentrated AI equity exposure.

**FX / rates implications**
- Rising UST yields and a Treasury seen as intervening ad hoc (vs. "regular and predictable" issuance) raises long-end risk premium — a headwind for EM carry trades funded off low US rates and a potential USD support/volatility driver.
- Oil spike from Iran tensions (Strait of Hormuz risk) is a stagflationary EM risk: negative for Asia oil importers (INR, PHP, IDR current accounts) and supportive for LATAM oil exporters (COP, MXN via Pemex linkages) at the margin.
- Sanctions threat targeting China's Iran oil trade adds a fresh US-China friction vector, a risk factor for CNY/CNH and broader Asia FX sentiment.
- Persistent US fiscal/debt concerns and "financial repression" talk (artificially low rates) support structural USD debasement/gold narratives relevant to EM reserve and hedging flows.

**Watch list**
- Size and cadence of Treasury's expanded long-bond buybacks; next 20-year/30-year auction.
- Fiscal consolidation announcement from Bessent/Vought, expected late this week or early next week.
- Iran/Strait of Hormuz developments and any Chinese response to US sanctions threats on Iran oil trade.
- 10-year (~4.70%) and 30-year (~5.33% recent high) yield levels for further backup or stabilization.

episodes.title: Why US Equity Returns Are Broadening Beyond AI Stocks
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Goldman Sachs' ETF/vol trading head Sean Titasia discusses why US equity returns are broadening beyond mega-cap AI stocks, driven by strong Q2 earnings and falling uncertainty, while flagging bond-market supply pressures and the upcoming Jackson Hole symposium as key macro risks. Relevant mainly as a US risk-sentiment and rates-supply barometer that feeds into global carry and USD conditions.

**Key points**
- Q2 earnings season ~92% complete; 64% of reporters beat estimates by more than one standard deviation, one of the highest beat rates on record; 2027 consensus EPS lifted ~2% to $390-400.
- Equal-weight S&P has outperformed the regular S&P by ~300bps YTD as the rally broadens beyond the "Magnificent Seven"; median stock earnings growth is 14% YoY, the largest since post-COVID.
- VIX fell from ~21 (end July) to 15; implied correlation at the S&P index level is near all-time lows, making index hedges/options cheap.
- Rising oil prices and heavy global bond supply (US hyperscaler capex, European defense spending, Japanese fiscal expansion) are pressuring the back end of yield curves; US Treasury signaled increasing buyback program size, which stabilized long-end yields.
- GS research flags a possible H2 growth slowdown versus H1.

**FX / rates implications**
- Global supply of long-dated government bonds (US, Europe, Japan) pressuring back-end yields is a risk factor for DM and EM term premia and could spill into EM local-currency rates if UST 10y sells off further.
- Rising oil prices are a watch item for inflation-sensitive EM importers (INR, PHP, IDR, TRY-like credits) versus exporters (COP, MXN via broader risk channel).
- Falling VIX and cheap index correlation/hedging costs signal a supportive backdrop for carry trades broadly, including EM FX carry, as long as risk sentiment holds.
- Fed policy uncertainty (33% probability priced for a July hike, highest since 1990) and new Fed Chair Worsh's data-dependent, no-forward-guidance stance add two-way risk to USD and UST yields into Jackson Hole.

**Watch list**
- Jackson Hole next week: new Fed Chair Worsh's first framework-setting remarks, critical for gauging Fed reaction function and USD/UST direction.
- Path of oil prices and long-end UST/Bund/JGB yields amid heavy global sovereign bond supply.
- US Treasury buyback program details and their effect on back-end yield stability.
- Incoming US labor market data (unemployment rate, claims) for signs of H2 growth slowdown.

episodes.title: What is Hong Kong's Northern Metropolis?
episodes.feed: Under the Banyan Tree (HSBC Global Research)
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
HSBC's Under the Banyan Tree podcast discusses Hong Kong's Northern Metropolis, a ~$400 billion (HK$3 trillion), 20-year mega-development on the Shenzhen border designed to house up to 2.5 million people across an area five times the size of Manhattan. It's a regional infrastructure/demographic story rather than a direct FX or rates catalyst, but touches on Greater Bay Area integration, capital markets, and HKD/USD peg dynamics.

**Key points**
- Project cost estimated at ~HK$3 trillion (~$400bn), roughly five times last year's Hong Kong budget.
- Timeline is around 20 years; MTR stations opening next year, a data center breaking ground and completing in ~3 years, developers already launching projects.
- Around 1 million people already live in the north; the plan is to add roughly 1-1.5 million more, not a full 2.5 million from scratch.
- Funding model blends government-built infrastructure (MTR etc.) with private capital; developers are forming consortiums to share risk in early tenders.
- Talent gap is central: Shenzhen has ~2 million tech workers versus Hong Kong's ~500,000, and the project aims to leverage Shenzhen's talent pool via Greater Bay Area integration.
- Hong Kong offers a USD-denominated capital-raising venue distinct from Shenzhen's RMB market, positioning it as a fundraising hub for mainland tech firms.
- Aligns with Beijing's 15th Five-Year Plan and Hong Kong's own five-year plan; framed as addressing Hong Kong's aging demographics.

**FX / rates implications**
- Explicitly noted that attracting private capital is harder given current US rate trajectory uncertainty, linking project financing costs to Fed policy expectations.
- Long-dated, HKD-denominated capex program with USD fundraising angle underscores Hong Kong's continued role as an offshore USD/CNH-adjacent funding hub tied to the currency board/peg system.
- No direct near-term HKD peg, CNH, or rates trading signal; relevance is structural/long-horizon (Greater Bay Area integration, HK-China capital market linkage) rather than immediately tradable.

**Watch list**
- MTR station openings in the Northern Metropolis next year as a delivery milestone.
- Data center completion in ~3 years as a concrete project progress marker.
- Ongoing developer tenders/consortium formations as a gauge of private capital appetite amid the US rate environment.

episodes.title: EV sales slow, US Treasury yields grow, 'Niu Lai' has impressive box office mojo
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A Planet Money Indicator roundup covering three unrelated stories: a slump in US EV sales even as EV demand rises globally, a jump in the 30-year US Treasury yield to a near two-decade high, and a viral low-budget Chinese animated film's box-office success. The Treasury yield story is the most relevant for a macro/rates trader given the fiscal and AI-driven debt-supply dynamics discussed.

**Key points**
- US EV sales fell 27% year-over-year since last July even as global EV sales rose over 10%, following the Trump administration's ending of the federal EV purchase incentive last September; battery factories (e.g., Ford, GM, LG) are pivoting toward grid-scale storage batteries to serve data-center demand.
- The 30-year US Treasury yield is at 5.3%, its highest level in nearly two decades.
- Drivers cited: US national debt just surpassed $40 trillion, raising investor risk perceptions; and "hyperscaler" tech companies are issuing large volumes of corporate debt (e.g., Amazon's 31-year bonds yield roughly a percentage point above comparable Treasuries) to fund AI/data-center buildouts, potentially crowding out Treasury demand.
- The US Treasury announced a large bond buyback intended to inject liquidity and lower interest rates; market reaction so far described as muted.
- A Chinese animated film, "Niu Lai" (roughly "the cow arrives"), reportedly made on a shoestring budget by a mother-son duo over five years, went viral and earned about 29 million yuan (~$4.2 million) in its first weeks after an initial negative reception turned positive online.

**FX / rates implications**
- Rising long-end UST yields amid heavy federal and hyperscaler corporate issuance is a global rates driver — higher US term premium/borrowing costs can pressure risk sentiment and tighten financial conditions relevant to EM local-currency debt and carry trades.
- No direct EM Asia/LATAM currency or central bank commentary in this episode.

**Watch list**
- Further Treasury buyback operations and their effect on long-end yields.
- Corporate bond issuance trends from hyperscalers as a signal of crowding-out pressure on sovereign debt markets.

episodes.title: US Rates: Treasury Buyback Expansion
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
J.P. Morgan's rates strategy team unpacks the U.S. Treasury's surprise off-cycle announcement to double long-end buyback operation sizes (10-20y and 20-30y buckets) starting September, a highly unusual move outside the normal quarterly refunding process. The team argues this signals discomfort with rising long-end yields rather than any genuine liquidity need, with implications for fiscal credibility and global rates.

**Key points**
- Buyback max sizes doubling from $2bn to at least $4bn per operation, adding ~$14-16bn/quarter (~$64bn annualized) — small relative to the ~$5tn gross coupon issuance and $31tn Treasury market.
- JPM's proprietary buyback scoring framework (offer-to-max ratio, off-the-run dispersion, liquidity preference) shows no fundamental justification for the change — all metrics near multi-year average/best levels.
- 30y yields up ~40bp over recent weeks; long end rallied on the news then fully reversed the next day.
- Budget deficit stable at 6% of GDP for over a year; no accompanying fiscal consolidation announced, raising credibility concerns about debt management strategy.
- Global yields (particularly Japan, worth ~20bp of the move) are now transmitting into UST yields, a reversal from the prior decade when low/negative global yields anchored Treasuries.
- Analogy drawn to UK 2022 LDI-crisis debt management interventions: announcement effects are real but short-lived without fundamental/fiscal follow-through.

**FX / rates implications**
- USD/UST: Signals Treasury/Administration discomfort with high long rates ahead of midterm elections; risk of more aggressive steps (cutting long-end auction sizes) that could flatten the curve short-term but likely prove non-durable absent fiscal consolidation — bearish credibility for USD rates markets if perceived as unfunded intervention.
- JGB linkage: BoJ monetary normalization pace cited as a key external driver of UST long-end yields — any acceleration in Japan hiking could ease upward pressure on US long rates, an important cross-asset carry consideration.
- No direct monetary base/inflation impact seen (composition shift only), so limited read-through to Fed policy path, but a smaller Fed balance sheet (with maturity roll-off shifted short) could still mean higher/steeper curves ahead.

**Watch list**
- Swap spreads and off-the-run liquidity metrics as gauges of whether this becomes a lasting shift.
- Potential further Treasury action: cutting long-end auction sizes if curve steepening persists.
- Fed balance-sheet task force conclusions expected by year-end.
- U.S. midterm elections in ~2.5 years as a political backdrop to rate-lowering pressure.

episodes.title: Heatwaves and waterways
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
FT Unhedged discusses how a summer heatwave and drought have collapsed water levels on the Rhine, Germany's main freight artery, disrupting industrial supply chains and denting German growth forecasts. Not a core EM story, but a live illustration of climate-driven supply shocks feeding into eurozone growth and inflation, relevant background for anyone pricing ECB and EUR risk.

**Key points**
- Rhine water level near Kaub has fallen to about 1 meter versus a normal 1.9-2.1 meters, cutting barge capacity to roughly a third of normal load.
- The Rhine carries 80% of Germany's domestic shipping; a similar 2018 drought wiped out an estimated 0.4% of GDP that year.
- Bundesbank warned of supply-chain disruption and a meaningful hit to industrial production; Oxford Economics estimates a 0.2% GDP hit in Q3; ING sees the Rhine issue cutting 0.3 percentage points off Germany's already-modest 0.5% 2026 growth forecast.
- Deepening the shallow Kaub section has been in federal planning since 1992 and is now not expected until 2033; Germany has suspended its Sunday truck ban to ease congestion, with limited effect given lorry driver shortages and regulated rest hours.
- Barclays analysis flagged accelerating food-price inflation from drought-hit harvests; some German farmers expect total crop losses.

**FX / rates implications**
- Marginal negative for EUR/growth narrative: recurring climate-driven supply disruptions are a small but persistent drag on German industrial output and a source of eurozone food-inflation upside risk, a factor for ECB watchers even if not decisive.
- No direct EM Asia/LATAM read-through; relevant mainly as a template for how commodity-transport bottlenecks (rivers, ports) can move into inflation and growth data elsewhere.

**Watch list**
- German Q3 GDP prints for confirmation of the Rhine-related drag.
- Further Bundesbank commentary on supply-chain and industrial production impact.
- Food-price inflation data in Germany/eurozone following drought-damaged harvests.

episodes.title: At Any Rate - Global FX: Debate Corner 2.0
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
JPMorgan's global FX team debates the dollar's sharp reaction to the US Treasury's move to increase long-end bond buybacks this quarter, which flattened the UST curve and triggered a broad dollar sell-off. The panel weighs whether this reflects a genuine easing-of-financial-conditions channel or a more concerning policy-unpredictability/credibility premium reminiscent of 2025's dollar-debasement trade, with implications for carry positioning across G10 and EM.

**Key points**
- Treasury's buyback increase (~$14bn this quarter vs a $32trn UST market) followed a sequence of signals: yen intervention, a FEMA repo facility for Japan, and surprise issuance guidance changes, read by the team as neutral-to-dollar-negative rather than a shock.
- Fed hike pricing for the next year is little changed (~35-37bp), unlike 2025 when rising term premium coincided with an actual Fed easing bias, making the team skeptical the current sell-off is durable.
- US financial conditions are already the loosest in years, limiting room for a middle-of-the-smile dollar sell-off comparable to 2025's debasement episode.
- Jackson Hole (Chair Powell) and upcoming core PCE (Feroli forecast 0.32% m/m) flagged as key tests for the Fed-terminal-rate thesis.
- Carry theme reinforced: bullish NOK and AUD, and JPMorgan's EM team still constructive on COP, funded via short CHF and SEK given Riksbank pushback on hikes and stretched Swiss positioning.
- CAD bias turns less bearish given better data and prospects of lower US tariffs, though it remains a preferred funder for long EM carry trades.

**FX / rates implications**
- Dollar view stays watchfully neutral; a durable dollar-negative move requires the Fed terminal rate to actually come down, not just a term-premium rise.
- Rising UST term premium without falling front-end rates is not the toxic dollar combo seen in 2025, capping downside conviction on USD.
- EM carry (long COP) funded via CHF/SEK remains a favored expression; broader EM FX benefits if UST term premium eases without Fed credibility concerns escalating.

**Watch list**
- Jackson Hole speech (Powell), next week.
- Core PCE print, Feroli forecasts 0.32% m/m.
- September BoJ meeting and any MOF/GPIF-related yen developments.
- Riksbank commentary on its hiking cycle amid sub-1% core CPI.

episodes.title: Global Data Pod: Western Europe motors on
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
J.P. Morgan's Global Data Pod reviews August flash PMIs for the Euro area and UK against a backdrop of renewed Middle East-driven energy price increases and European drought/low-water conditions affecting river shipping. The data show resilient Western European growth even as central banks weigh sticky-but-moderating inflation signals, informing the near-term ECB, BoE, Riksbank and Scandinavian rate paths.

**Key points**
- Euro area composite PMI ticked up in August, signaling growth near 1.4-1.5%, close to J.P. Morgan's 1.25% forecast with modest upside risk; UK PMI held up better than expected after a large July increase.
- Growth is unbalanced: Germany and France (especially services) are weak versus strong periphery gains skewed to Spain; German manufacturing PMI output has risen ~6 points over three releases, linked to data-center buildout and defense/fiscal spending.
- Euro area PMI employment index improved broadly in August, signaling jobs growth potentially above 0.5% against ~1% growth potential.
- Euro area PMI output/input price indices moderated for a third straight month despite higher energy prices, consistent with ~2.5% inflation; HICP core running near 2.6%, but ex-tech-prices and German medicine-price noise, closer to 2.1%.
- No evidence yet of energy-price pass-through into core HICP; only a few tenths of upward pressure expected by year-end.
- UK output price index stayed sticky/rose, aligning with an upside surprise in UK core inflation this week.

**FX / rates implications**
- A September ECB hike is viewed as a near-done deal and fully priced; a further hike late in the year remains a live but not base-case risk, capping EUR upside from rate differentials alone.
- BoE, Riksbank and other Scandinavian central banks are seen delivering hikes by year-end, with firmer PMIs raising the chance these get pulled forward — modestly GBP/SEK/NOK supportive.
- Persistent Middle East-driven energy price gains remain a global inflation/risk-sentiment input relevant to broader FX and commodity-linked EM currencies, though pass-through so far looks orderly, not disorderly.

**Watch list**
- September ECB Governing Council meeting (hike largely priced).
- Bank of England November meeting for a potential hike.
- Upcoming Euro area/UK HICP and core inflation prints for confirmation of moderating pricing signals.
- European Commission confidence survey (August) for corroboration of PMI price signals.

episodes.title: Beyond the fundamentals: How commodity markets are being impacted globally
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
McKeany-Flavell's commodity analysts move "beyond the fundamentals" to argue that geopolitics, freight disruption, biofuel demand, and macro/currency dynamics are now dominating agricultural and energy commodity pricing more than weather alone. For a macro trader, the episode is a useful cross-asset read on how two live wars (Russia-Ukraine, and an Iran conflict that began late February) are transmitting into energy, food inflation, freight costs, USD reserve-currency dynamics and the yen carry trade.

**Key points**
- Poor global growing conditions (drought/heat in Europe, wildfires in Indonesia's Kalimantan hitting palm/PKO/cocoa, fires in Brazil and Central Africa) are tightening ag-commodity supply into the 2026/27 marketing year.
- Biofuel demand (biodiesel, renewable diesel, ethanol) is surging across US, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Europe, and Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia), drawing down vegetable-oil stocks and tightening the crude-oil/veg-oil correlation.
- Wars in Ukraine/Russia and Iran have militarized key transit chokepoints (Black Sea, Arabian Sea, Caspian, Baltic, South China Sea, Strait of Hormuz), raising freight costs and impairing grain/energy exports; repeated strikes on energy infrastructure are structurally supportive of crude, diesel and natural gas.
- US debt held by the public has surpassed 100% of GDP, with debt service now the second-largest government expenditure after Social Security; ~80% of global equity market cap is US-based; oil is 15% of global trade and priced in USD; ~90% of the $7tn/day FX market has USD on one side.
- Speaker flags the "collapse of the yen spread trade" and chatter about Middle East oil being priced outside USD (even crypto) as signs the dollar's reserve role is being questioned.

**FX / rates implications**
- Sustained geopolitical/energy-driven inflation and a weakening USD reserve-currency narrative support a broad case for commodity-linked EM currencies (BRL, COP, MYR, IDR, CLP, PEN) as inflation hedges, while pressuring USD-denominated debt costs.
- Rising US fiscal debt/GDP and questions about UST safe-haven status could push managed money to rotate from Treasuries toward commodities, a theme relevant to UST 10y positioning and broader EM risk appetite.
- Yen carry-trade unwind risk is a direct volatility channel for EM Asia FX funded via JPY (IDR, INR, PHP, MYR), and for broader risk sentiment.
- Elevated freight/insurance costs and energy price support flow through to EM Asia importers (India, Philippines, Indonesia) reliant on imported tropical oils and energy.

**Watch list**
- Northern Hemisphere harvest data over coming weeks for wheat, corn, oilseeds, cocoa and coffee.
- Further escalation or de-escalation in Black Sea/Strait of Hormuz shipping and energy-infrastructure strikes.
- Signals on whether oil trade shifts away from USD pricing, and any further deterioration in the yen carry trade.

episodes.title: Through the noise: Watching Warsh at Jackson Hole
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This Standard Chartered weekly reviews the US Treasury's surprise move to nearly double buybacks of 10-30 year bonds after the 30-year yield hit its highest since 2007, plus the run-up to the Fed's Jackson Hole symposium next week. For an EM FX/rates trader, the direction of US yields, the dollar and Fed guidance under new leadership are the key global transmission channels into EM Asia and LATAM.

**Key points**
- US Treasury raised long-bond buybacks (10-30yr) to almost $4bn, with Secretary Bessent pledging more if needed, after 30yr yields hit levels last seen in 2007.
- Move is modest versus the $30tn stock of marketable Treasuries, unlikely to durably cap yields; drivers are rising US debt (national debt just crossed $40trn), monetary policy uncertainty under Fed Chair Warsh, and heavy AI hyperscaler bond issuance.
- Soft payrolls, cooling inflation and weak retail sales support a view that inflation peaked in Q2; PCE methodology revisions (effective September) should retroactively lower core PCE over the past five years, with core inflation seen reaching 2% by 2027, enabling Fed holds this year and cuts in 2027.
- All eyes on Jackson Hole next week for signals on the Fed's reaction function/rate-hold duration.
- Strong AI-driven US earnings season; StanChart raised AI capex forecasts to $750bn (+85% y/y) in 2026 and $1trn by 2027, lifting long-term capex CAGR assumption to 33% (2025-2030).
- China Q2 earnings solid (2026 EPS growth upgraded to 12.5% y/y) led by AI infrastructure, pharma, energy and autos (export-led); consumer/property still weak; StanChart stays overweight China equities.

**FX / rates implications**
- US dollar expected to act as the "pressure release valve" for fiscal/yield pressures — ongoing broad dollar softness (DXY) supports EM Asia and LATAM currencies generally and is a tailwind for carry trades.
- Preference for 3-5yr UST maturities over long bonds on continued disinflation and a softening labor market; long-end yields seen range-bound rather than falling sharply.
- Softer dollar seen sustaining the gold rally; range-bound (not rising) UST yields is a positive backdrop for risk assets/equities, supportive of broader risk sentiment relevant to EM flows.
- GBPUSD at a 3-month high driven mainly by broad USD weakness (not UK strength) — UK unemployment at 4.9%, wage growth slowing to 2.8%, but headline inflation rose to 2.9% y/y in July, leaving BoE facing stagflationary cross-currents; cable capped near 1.36 with consolidation risk toward 1.35.

**Watch list**
- Fed Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech next week for reaction-function clarity and rate-path signals.
- End-September US PCE methodology revisions and their retroactive effect on core inflation readings.
- GBPUSD near-term resistance around 1.36 and consolidation risk toward 1.35.
- Pace of AI-related bond issuance from hyperscalers and its impact on long-end UST supply/yields.

episodes.title: The Week Ahead - Hole-ding Out for a Hero
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Nomura's Week Ahead covers a calmer summer market backdrop dominated by Fed Chair Kevin Worsh's Jackson Hole speech, European political risk from rising right-wing populism, and three Asian central bank decisions (Korea, Thailand, Philippines) plus Singapore inflation — all directly relevant to EM Asia rates and global risk sentiment.

**Key points**
- Treasury Secretary Bessent announced longer-dated Treasury buybacks to ease upward pressure on US yields; DXY has weakened to its lowest since May.
- Worsh's Jackson Hole speech (Friday) expected to focus on Fed's broad intellectual framework (balance sheet policy, AI productivity, communication reform) rather than near-term policy signals; core PCE next week expected at 0.23% m/m.
- Nomura's US team sees election-cycle history (1994, 2002, 2016) supporting a Fed hold into US midterms, reinforcing their indefinite-hold call.
- US-Canada trade deal progress: proposal to cut tariffs on Canadian steel/aluminum to 25% and reduce auto duties; Nomura turning less bearish CAD.
- European political risk: French presidential election April 2026, Italian elections possibly brought forward; Le Pen's best polling position yet but has dropped Frexit rhetoric; ECB house view is a 25bp hike in September, with hawkish upside risk from Brent (~$94/bbl) and European gas (~€65-66) amid Iran-related escalation.
- Asia: Bank of Korea expected to hike 25bp (2027 growth forecast to be revised up to 2.6% from 2.1%, a hawkish signal), with two more 25bp hikes seen in October and February; Bank of Thailand expected to hold unanimously; BSP expected to hike 25bp for a third straight meeting on above-target inflation; Singapore core CPI for July expected to jump to 2.3% from 1.6% on electricity tariff hikes and demand-side pressure.

**FX / rates implications**
- KRW: hawkish BoK bias (rate hike plus upgraded 2027 growth) supportive; watch dissent count for near-term dovish tell.
- PHP: hawkish BSP tone supports further tightening path, PHP rates upside.
- THB: BOT on hold all year, looking through supply-side inflation — rate-neutral stance.
- SGD: MAS likely to stay vigilant on inflation given sharp core CPI pickup.
- EUR: ECB hawkish tilt (September hike, gas/oil-driven inflation risk) supportive of EUR; French political risk a tail factor into 2026.
- CAD: less bearish given US-Canada trade deal progress.
- USD/DXY: softer post-Bessent buyback announcement and Treasury yield relief.

**Watch list**
- Kevin Worsh's Jackson Hole speech, Friday.
- ECB September meeting (house view: 25bp hike).
- BoK, BOT, BSP decisions this week; Singapore July core CPI print.
- French presidential election, April 2026; Italian election timing.
